---
title: "Designing an Internal Audit Program"
order: 77

## The debrief nobody wanted to have

The AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) on-site assessor left
two days ago. The one nonconformance the visit produced — LAB-07's missing criterion-4
fitness-for-use documentation — closed inside the resolution window: your Quality Analyst
(QA) submitted a dated qualification review, and accreditation continued for another
two-year cycle. By every measure that matters externally, this reassessment was a success.

You called the debrief anyway, and you open it with a question your QA wasn't expecting.

"The assessor's own self-assessment tool found LAB-07's gap in APEX. DI-0301 — your own
data-integrity self-assessment — found the same gap, independently, months earlier. I'm
glad both of those worked. I want to know why our *internal audit program* didn't find it
first. That instrument has been checking Lakeshore's quality system for years. Equipment
fitness-for-use review is exactly the kind of thing it's supposed to catch."

She doesn't have a comfortable answer, and to her credit, she doesn't invent one. "Our
audit calendar checks every site and every process area on roughly the same schedule.
Nobody ever sat down and decided LAB-07's area, or Fairview generally, deserved a tighter
interval than, say, Brookfield's. And when an audit *does* touch equipment records, the
auditor pulls whatever's quickest to find and calls it a sample. There's no real rule
about who's independent enough to run which audit, no training record showing anyone was
ever taught audit technique specifically, and no consistent scale for how serious a
finding is once one turns up. We have an audit program in the sense that audits happen.
We don't have one in the sense that it's actually built to find the next LAB-07 before
someone else does."

That's the honest diagnosis, and it's this module's whole job to fix. `internal-audits-
and-management-review` already told you what an internal audit *is* — a planned, periodic,
independent check that practice matches documentation — and told you, by name, that
independence is a property the audit has to have without showing you how to build it.
This module builds the missing layer: who's allowed to audit what, what makes someone
qualified to do it, which processes and sites get checked more often, how a sample
actually has to be chosen to mean anything, and how a finding gets sorted by how serious
it actually is. You'll build all four pieces against Lakeshore's real situation — LAB-07's
now-closed history as the cautionary example, and Fairview's paper-file practice as the
live risk sitting in front of you right now.

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure mode a weak internal audit program produces, and it's subtler than
"no audits happen." Lakeshore's audits *did* happen, on schedule, with a report at the
end of each one — and they still missed a real, multi-year gap that an outside tool
caught twice before the internal program ever did. A program that runs on a fixed
calendar, staffed by whoever's available, sampling whatever's convenient, and grading
every finding the same way isn't broken in any way that shows up on an audit log. It's
broken in the one way that actually counts: it isn't built to find what it doesn't
already expect to find.

You already know this exact failure mode by a different name. A vulnerability-scanning
program that scans every system on the same interval, run by whoever's on the rotation
that week, without weighting internet-facing or legacy systems any higher than anything
else, "runs" in every sense an audit trail can prove — and still misses the one legacy
box nobody's looked at hard in years, right up until someone else finds it first. The fix
in your world isn't "scan more." It's risk-based asset tiering, named scanner
qualifications, a defined sampling approach instead of "whatever's open," and a severity
scale that actually changes what happens next. This module builds the identical four
pieces, for the identical reason, on top of a practice — internal audit — you already
know exists but have never had to design yourself.

One line of continuity worth naming before you build any of this: your QA's independence
on a *quality decision* — a disposition, a reportability call, a CAPA (corrective and
preventive action) sign-off — is a control you already protect deliberately, covered in
`directing-the-quality-analyst`. Auditor independence is that same muscle, aimed at a
different question: not "can anyone override her disposition," but "is the person
checking a process's paper trail ever the same person who built or runs that process."
Same principle, new application. This module doesn't redevelop the first one — it builds
the second.

## The rule in plain English

Four pieces, each one a real design decision for Lakeshore, not an abstract definition.

**1. Auditor independence — a concrete rule, not a slogan.** "The auditor isn't the
person who did the work" has to resolve to an actual test someone can apply before an
audit is assigned. Lakeshore's rule: **an auditor may not audit a process they directly
perform, a site they operationally manage, or a system or record they personally
approved, signed, or configured within the audit's look-back period.** Your QA can audit
Brookfield's donor-eligibility records, because she doesn't run Brookfield day to day.
She cannot audit a validation package she signed as quality approver, or a CAPA she
closed herself — that's not a different person checking the work, it's the same person
checking their own work twice. For a quality team as small as Lakeshore's, where one
person sometimes has to both do the work and eventually audit somewhere nearby, the rule
needs a release valve: when no internal staff member clears the independence test for a
given area, Lakeshore brings in a contracted or cross-trained auditor from outside that
area's chain, rather than quietly waiving the rule for convenience.

**2. Auditor competency — two different kinds, both required, neither optional.**
Someone qualified to audit BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) validation
records needs real working familiarity with what a validation package should contain —
otherwise they can confirm a signature exists without ever noticing the signature is
dated after the system went live. That's process knowledge. Separately, that same person
needs training in audit technique itself: how to plan a sample, how to ask a question
that doesn't lead the witness, how to write a finding that states what was observed
against what was expected, not an opinion. A subject-matter expert who's never been
taught to audit will often find nothing, not because nothing's wrong, but because they
don't know how to look. Lakeshore's fix: a simple competency record per auditor — which
process areas they're qualified to audit, and when they last completed audit-technique
training — checked before an assignment goes out, not assumed because someone has
seniority.

**3. Risk-based audit scheduling — the calendar your debrief just found missing.** This
is a direct callback to `quality-risk-management`'s risk ranking and filtering: sort
audit subjects into bins — high, medium, low — using factors that actually predict where
a gap is likely to be hiding, then audit the high bin more often. For Lakeshore, that
means weighing site and process risk honestly instead of treating every subject as
interchangeable. Fairview scores higher than Brookfield on this exercise for a specific,
nameable reason: its downtime SOP binder and several other quality records still live on
paper rather than fully inside BECS, which makes drift between the record and reality
easier to miss between audits. Legacy equipment like LAB-07 scores higher too — older
instruments with a thinner, less automated maintenance trail are exactly where a
documentation gap survives longest unnoticed. A flat, same-interval calendar treats
Fairview's paper binders and Brookfield's current BECS records as equally easy to verify.
They aren't, and the schedule should say so.

**4. Evidence sampling — large and representative enough to mean something, not a
handful of convenient records.** An audit can't check every record a process has
produced, and it doesn't need to — but the sample it does check has to be big enough,
and chosen well enough, that a clean result actually supports a conclusion about the
*whole* population, not just the few records someone happened to grab. Pulling the three
easiest-to-find fitness-for-use files and calling the whole equipment population
confirmed is not a sample; it's a guess with a checkbox next to it. This is exactly where
Fairview's paper-file practice bites hardest. BECS's electronic records can be filtered
and pulled as a genuine random subset in minutes. A box of paper binders can't — pulling
a defensible sample from them takes real, deliberate selection, not whatever's on top.
An auditor assigned to Fairview needs to plan the sample before walking in, not improvise
it once there, and the plan needs to say how many records, selected how, and why that's
enough to support a conclusion about everything Fairview holds, not just what got
checked.

**5. Nonconformance grading — a scale with teeth, not a single "finding" bucket.**
Lakeshore's internal audit findings get sorted into three tiers, each with its own clock
and its own escalation path:

- **Critical** — a finding tied to an immediate patient-safety signal, or one that
  independently triggers a reportability question. Same-day containment, immediate
  escalation to you and to Quality leadership, full investigation opened now, not at the
  next audit meeting.
- **Major** — a real, systemic gap in a control that's supposed to be working, with no
  patient-safety event yet, but a genuine mechanism failure. A defined short window — 30
  calendar days is Lakeshore's own choice here, not a cited number — to reach a
  disposition and open a CAPA if the root cause is systemic.
- **Minor** — an isolated documentation or process gap, unlikely on its own to indicate a
  broader failure. Logged, trended, and fixed on a longer timeline — Lakeshore's own
  choice of 90 days — with one real teeth: **three Minor findings against the same
  process within a year escalate the whole pattern to Major**, so a slow accumulation of
  small gaps can't sit forever under a label that never forces real action.

Run LAB-07's now-closed history back through this scale, honestly, as the worked example
it is. A documented fitness-for-use gap on equipment that still passed every daily
quality-control check, with no patient-safety event behind it, is **Major**, not
Critical — real and systemic, but not an active safety signal. Under a 30-day Major
clock, a program built this way would have forced a disposition on LAB-07's gap on its
own schedule, years before AABB's self-assessment tool or DI-0301 ever had to find it for
Lakeshore. That's not a reason to reopen LAB-07 — it's closed, correctly, on its own
timeline. It's the argument for why this module exists at all.

One more instrument worth naming once, not redeveloping: `directing-the-quality-analyst`
gave you the cold-read test and gap triage — *must fix before I sign*, *fix going
forward*, *fine as is* — for reviewing a document's own defensibility. Nonconformance
grading is a related but separate judgment: not "is this write-up good enough to sign,"
but "how serious is the underlying gap this audit just found, and how fast does it have
to move." Different question, same underlying discipline of sorting findings instead of
treating them all alike.

## Citation decoder

Every row below is labeled the same way, deliberately: **industry practice (ASQ Certified
Quality Auditor body-of-knowledge themes) — described in this curriculum's own words, not
a cited standard.** No ASQ section number, exam-objective number, or body-of-knowledge
text is quoted or cited anywhere in this module, the same handling this curriculum has
always given GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice) and AABB Standards text. This
module introduces no new regulation, guidance, or standard.

| Row | Tier | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| Auditor independence | Industry practice (ASQ CQA themes) | The rule that disqualifies an auditor from checking their own work or their own area — Lakeshore's own worded version above. |
| Auditor competency | Industry practice (ASQ CQA themes) | Process knowledge plus audit technique, both required, tracked per auditor. |
| Risk-based audit scheduling | Industry practice (ASQ CQA themes) | The bin-and-frequency logic built directly on `quality-risk-management`'s risk ranking and filtering. |
| Evidence sampling | Industry practice (ASQ CQA themes) | The general principle of a defensible sample — no statistical formula cited or implied. |
| Nonconformance grading | Industry practice (ASQ CQA themes) | Lakeshore's own three-tier scale, its own choice of labels and timelines. |
| 21 CFR 606.100(c) | Regulation — already quoted in full in `internal-audits-and-management-review` | A thorough, recorded investigation of any discrepancy, regardless of how it was found. Referenced here, not re-quoted. |

## The actual text

There is almost no text to quote in this module, and that's by design, not an omission.
ASQ's Certified Quality Auditor body of knowledge is a real, respected professional
framework behind the themes this module builds on — independence, competency, risk-based
planning, sampling, severity grading — but it's proprietary exam content, not a public
regulatory or standards text this curriculum can quote or cite by section number, the
same handling already given to GAMP 5's own copyrighted guidance. Naming the themes
honestly, in Lakeshore's own words, is the correct and complete citation here. There is
no fake section number to invent, and this module doesn't invent one.

The one piece of regulatory text underneath all of it is the same sentence
`internal-audits-and-management-review` already quoted in full from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`:

> A thorough investigation, including the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained
> discrepancy or the failure of a lot or unit to meet any of its specifications shall be
> made and recorded.

Read it the same way that module already taught you to: an audit finding is a deviation
discovered through a particular channel, and it owes that same investigation-and-record
floor regardless of which tier this module's own grading scale assigns it. A **Minor**
finding still gets a recorded investigation. It just doesn't get the same clock or the
same escalation path a **Critical** one does.

## What an assessor or inspector would actually look for

Not whether Lakeshore's internal audit program exists — that part is easy to confirm.
What a sharp reviewer actually probes is whether the program is *built* to find things,
and that comes down to four concrete artifacts.

**An audit calendar that shows its own risk logic.** Not just dates and sites, but a
visible reason Fairview and legacy-equipment areas sit in a tighter rotation than
lower-risk subjects — and evidence the calendar was actually kept, not just drafted.

**Auditor qualification records, checked before assignment.** Process-area competency and
audit-technique training, both dated, for the specific person assigned to a specific
audit — not "she's senior, she can audit anything."

**A stated sampling plan per audit**, written before the auditor walks in: how many
records, selected how, from what population. An auditor who can't say why their sample
size was enough, or how the records were chosen, hasn't actually sampled anything — they
pulled whatever was easiest to find and are calling it representative after the fact.

**A nonconformance log that shows the grading tier actually drove the timeline.** A
Critical finding that sat for three weeks before anyone escalated it is worse than no
grading scale at all — it means Lakeshore wrote down a severity rule it doesn't actually
follow, which reads to an assessor as exactly the kind of "documented but not followed"
gap this curriculum has surfaced before.

## Common traps

**"Whoever's free that week audits whatever's due that week."** The single most common
way a paper audit program stays a paper audit program. Staffing by availability instead
of by independence-and-competency is how an auditor ends up checking a process they
helped build, or checking equipment records without ever having been taught what a
fitness-for-use file is actually supposed to contain. Availability answers "who has
time." It never answers "who's qualified and independent enough to find something real."

**Treating every finding as equally urgent, or equally unimportant.** Grading everything
"Critical" burns out an organization's own escalation path until nobody treats the label
as meaning anything — the same alarm fatigue you already know from a paging system that
cries wolf. Grading everything "Minor" is the opposite failure, and the one Lakeshore's
old program was quietly closer to: a real, systemic gap like LAB-07's sits for years
because nothing ever forced it onto a shorter clock. A grading scale only works if its
tiers actually produce different timelines and different escalation paths — and if
someone is checking, after the fact, that they did.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask to see the independence rule applied, not just written down.** A policy that says
  auditors must be independent and an audit roster that never actually tests anyone
  against that rule are two different things — ask who was disqualified from an
  assignment recently, and why.
- **Check that risk-based scheduling produced a real calendar difference, not just a
  sentence about risk.** If Fairview and Brookfield sit on the same interval anyway, the
  risk-ranking exercise was theater.
- **Ask what a sample actually looked like on the last audit that touched a paper-file
  site or process.** "We pulled a few records" is not an answer; "we pulled N records,
  selected this way, out of a population of this size" is.
- **Watch for a grading scale that exists on paper but doesn't change behavior.** A
  Critical finding that moved at Minor speed is the single fastest way to lose an
  assessor's confidence in the whole program.
- **Run LAB-07's own history as a standing lesson, not a closed file to forget.** The
  question worth asking of any new audit finding isn't just "how bad is this" — it's
  "would our *old* program have caught this before an outside reviewer did, and does our
  new one actually fix that."

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA proposes labeling Lakeshore's nonconformance tiers "Critical / Major / Minor," with a 30-day Major clock and a 90-day Minor clock. Is she required to use those exact labels and timelines because that's the industry-standard scale?

No — and this is worth being precise about. There is no single cited AABB, FDA, or ASQ
standard that fixes these labels or these timelines; this is industry practice, and the
exact labels and clocks are Lakeshore's own design choice, not a requirement imposed from
outside. What *is* expected, by any reviewer worth the name, is that whatever scale
Lakeshore picks actually produces different, enforced timelines and escalation paths per
tier — the specific words "Critical" and "Major" could just as easily be "Tier 1" and
"Tier 2" and nothing about the program's real strength would change.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: An auditor pulls the five most recently updated equipment files at Fairview, finds all five current, and reports "equipment records at Fairview are in good shape." Is that a defensible sample?

No. The five most recently updated files are the ones *least* likely to show a gap —
they were just touched. A defensible sample has to be drawn so it could actually surface
a problem if one exists: a genuinely representative cross-section of the equipment
population, not the subset most likely to already look clean. This is exactly the trap
Fairview's paper-file practice makes easy to fall into, since pulling a true cross-section
from paper binders takes deliberate planning that pulling the top few files on a shelf
does not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Your QA audited a CAPA she herself closed three months ago, reasoning that "enough time passed that it's basically a fresh look." Does that satisfy Lakeshore's auditor-independence rule?

No. The independence rule turns on *who did the work*, not on how much time has passed
since they did it. Lakeshore's own rule disqualifies an auditor from checking a system or
record they personally approved, signed, or configured within the audit's look-back
period — and closing the CAPA is exactly that kind of personal involvement. A delay
doesn't convert the same person into a different, independent reviewer. This audit needs
to go to someone else, or, if nobody internally clears the independence test for this
area, to an outside auditor brought in for exactly this gap.
:::

## Where this goes next

Lakeshore's internal audit program now has the four pieces it was missing: a real
independence rule, tracked competency, a calendar built on actual risk instead of a flat
interval, a sampling discipline strong enough to mean something even against Fairview's
paper files, and a grading scale that would have forced LAB-07's own gap onto a real
clock years before an outside reviewer found it. `mock-inspections-and-presenting-it-
becs-evidence` closes this course by putting all of it — this program, the AABB process,
the BPDR (Biological Product Deviation Report) filing, the 483 response — in front of a
reviewer actually in the room, and by resolving, out loud, what `data-integrity-and-
records` left open: DED-0458's "accurate" question and the deferred-donor-record cadence
decision.
